items.prompt: Define customer needs.
items.canonical_answer: Customer needs are the wants and requirements customers have for a product: what it does, how well it is made, what it costs, where it can be bought, and the service that comes with it.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must cover what the product does, its cost and where it can be bought, with the service around it. Naming one example, such as a low price, is not a definition.

items.prompt: A bakery in Windhoek plans a new lunch range. Explain why the bakery should identify what its customers want before it designs the range.
items.canonical_answer: Identifying needs first means the range is matched to demand from the start. Research - surveys, till records, watching what sells out by noon - shows what customers actually want to eat and what they will pay, so the bakery is less likely to spend money on a range nobody wants. Because each design choice, from price to packaging, answers evidence rather than a guess, the launch sells steadily and the research cost is recovered; without it, the bakery could fill its shelves with food its regulars walk past.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for identifying that research matches the range to demand, because products designed against evidence are less likely to fail. Second reason: award for the saving - the bakery is less likely to spend on food nobody wants.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main ways a business can find out what its customers need.
items.canonical_answer: Surveys and questionnaires ask customers directly and reach many people cheaply. Interviews and focus groups hear customers explain in their own words, giving depth a tick-box form cannot. Observation watches what customers actually do, which can differ from what they say. Records of past sales show what has really been bought, and complaints and feedback reveal needs the business is currently missing. What the set includes is a trade-off: surveys are broad but shallow, focus groups are deep but narrow, and a business that combines two or more of these features gets both reach and depth.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element named - surveys, focus groups or interviews, observation, sales records, feedback - and one mark for developing what each way includes, such as the difference between what customers say and what they do.

items.prompt: Define what is meant by satisfying customer needs.
items.canonical_answer: Satisfying customer needs means designing the product, its price, where it is sold and how it is promoted so that each matches what customers want and can afford.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must relate the product, price, availability and promotion to what customers want and can afford. Giving one example of a satisfied customer alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: Explain why a business that satisfies its customers' needs is likely to see those customers return.
items.canonical_answer: A satisfied customer has been given what they actually wanted: the product performed as expected, it was available where they shop and the price was within their means. Because nothing in the purchase disappointed them, they tend to buy again from the same business and to recommend it to others, which brings sales the business did not have to pay to win a second time. The purpose of satisfaction is exactly this: it turns a first sale into a stream of later ones.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the link - satisfaction means nothing disappointed the customer, because the purchase matched what they wanted. Second reason: award for repeat buying and recommendations arriving without further promotion cost.

items.prompt: Explain the elements that together make up customer satisfaction for a shop.
items.canonical_answer: Four elements work together. The product performs as the customer expected, which is the core of the promise. It is available where they usually shop, so finding it costs no effort. The price is within their means, so wanting it and affording it are the same thing. And the service around the sale is helpful, from advice before purchase to support after it. What the parts include is a single experience: a customer who meets all four walks out satisfied; a customer who meets three and is ignored at the counter often does not.
marking_guidance: Elements: award one mark for each part - performance, availability, price, service - and one mark for what the parts include together: satisfaction when all four hold, and its absence when one fails.

items.prompt: Define customer loyalty.
items.canonical_answer: Customer loyalty is the tendency of customers to keep buying from the same business rather than switching to rivals, even when those rivals offer something similar.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include repeat buying from the same business despite similar rival offers. A single repeat purchase alone is not loyalty.

items.prompt: Explain why a business might spend more effort keeping the customers it already has than on winning new ones.
items.canonical_answer: Keeping a customer usually costs less than winning a new one: a first-time buyer has to be attracted through promotion or discounts, while a returning customer comes back on their own decision. Loyal customers also spread recommendations that bring in further sales at no extra cost. So the purpose of loyalty work - quality, service, schemes, contact - is to protect the cheapest sales the business has, and the money saved by not chasing replacements can be spent improving what loyal customers already value.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for retention costing less than attraction, because promotion and discounts are not needed to bring a loyal customer back. Second reason: award for recommendations from loyal customers generating further sales without new spending.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main methods a business can use to maintain customer loyalty.
items.canonical_answer: Consistent quality comes first: the product is the same at every visit, so trust holds through every purchase. Good service before and after the sale matters just as much, because loyalty lives in how problems are handled. Loyalty schemes reward repeat buying directly - a card stamped for every tenth haircut makes returning rational. And staying in contact, such as a message when a usual brand returns to stock, keeps the business in the customer's mind between purchases. What the set includes is reliability in different forms: a reliable product, reliable service, a reliable reward and a reliable presence.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - consistent quality, service, loyalty schemes, keeping contact - and one mark for what the methods include in common: each gives the customer a reason to return.

items.prompt: Define what is meant by building customer relationships.
items.canonical_answer: Building customer relationships means a business works to know its customers, communicate with them and keep their trust over time, rather than treating each sale as a one-off exchange.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include knowing customers and keeping their trust over time, contrasted with one-off selling. Listing friendly staff alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: Explain why building long-term relationships with its customers can protect a business when a competitor opens nearby.
items.canonical_answer: A customer with a real relationship - a seller who knows them, remembers their usual order and fixes complaints without argument - is more likely to stay when a rival opens, and even to forgive an occasional mistake such as a late delivery. The reason is that switching now has a cost of its own: the customer would be leaving behind a business that has earned their trust, not just comparing prices on a shelf. Relationships therefore protect the sales a price war attacks first.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the relationship giving the customer a reason to stay, because trust and recognition are things a new rival cannot copy at opening. Second reason: award for mistakes being forgiven within a relationship, which protects sales when things go wrong.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the ways a business builds relationships with its customers.
items.canonical_answer: Reliable service is the foundation: the customer is handled well every time, not just at the first sale. Complaints are answered quickly and fairly, which builds more trust than a sale where nothing went wrong. Personal contact - a follow-up message, a reminder when a service is due - tells the customer they are known. And records of what each customer buy let the business tailor what it offers and says. What these parts include is attention: each one shows the customer that the business remembers them and cares how the purchase went.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - reliable service, complaint handling, personal contact, purchase records - and one mark for what the ways include at heart: showing the customer they are known.

items.prompt: Define customer spending patterns.
items.canonical_answer: Customer spending patterns are the ways consumers divide their spending between goods and services - what they buy, how much of it and how often - and these patterns change over time.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must cover what consumers buy, how much and how often, and note that the pattern changes over time. Naming one product trend alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: A new mine opens near a small town and the incomes of hundreds of households rise. Explain how this change could lead to a shift in what the town's shoppers buy, and how it could affect a local furniture store.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: household incomes in the town rise. Mechanism: as incomes rise, customers shift some spending toward quality, convenience and leisure - new furniture instead of second-hand, better brands instead of basics - because they now have money beyond essentials and credit becomes easier to obtain. Consequence: the furniture store's sales of new suites could rise strongly, and its sales records, if it tracks them monthly, will show the change early enough to reorder before the shelves empty. For the business the chain runs both ways: a store that notices the pattern can profit from the boom, while one that keeps ordering for the old pattern of demand is left with the wrong stock.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must be tied to the given starting point of rising household incomes. Mechanism: award for the why - rising incomes free spending beyond essentials, so the spending pattern shifts. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - rising new-stock sales or the risk of stocking for old patterns - and a stakeholder consequence for the shoppers who can now afford more.

facts: hundreds of households with rising incomes

items.prompt: Swakopfresh Supermarket's till records show bottled water sales grew by a fifth last year while cold-drink sales slipped. Explain what the records suggest about the store's customers, and what the store should do next.
items.canonical_answer: The facts here point to a shift in the pattern of what customers drink: water grew by a fifth over a full year while cold drinks slipped, which suggests customers are increasingly choosing what they see as the healthier option. The reasoning is that a shift across a whole year, not one hot week, indicates a lasting change in tastes rather than weather. The store's own records spotted it early, which is exactly what tracking sales is for. Conclusion: the store should give water more shelf space and prime chilled positioning, trial a wider water range, and keep reading the drinks figures monthly to check the trend holds before committing to a full refit.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the store's facts - water up by a fifth across the year, cold drinks slipping. Reasoning: award for the link from a year-long shift to a change in tastes rather than a brief fluctuation. Conclusion: award for a choice that follows the reasoning, such as re-shelving and continued monthly tracking.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main causes behind changes in customer spending patterns.
items.canonical_answer: Income is the first: rising incomes move spending toward quality and leisure, falling incomes move it back toward basics. Tastes and fashion shift next, often spread by media, so a product's popularity can rise and fade within a year. Technology replaces whole needs - smartphones absorbed spending that once went to cameras and music players. Relative prices matter as well: when a product becomes dearer than its substitutes, some spending moves to the alternative. And the population itself changes shape, so spending tends to shift toward the groups that are growing, such as older customers. What the causes include is a shared feature: each changes what customers want or can afford, and the pattern follows.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - income, tastes, technology, relative prices, population change - and one mark for what the causes include in common: each alters wants or affordability.

items.prompt: Define what is meant by changing customer needs for a business.
items.canonical_answer: Customer needs change when the wants and expectations customers hold - shaped by incomes, tastes and technology - shift, so what satisfied them before no longer does; a business that notices the change early has time to plan its response.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include needs shifting with incomes, tastes or technology, and the value of noticing the change early. Describing one new product alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: A hardware chain keeps the same tool range while its customers move to ordering online and buying cordless models. Explain how ignoring changing customer needs could lead to falling sales for the chain, and how an early response could affect its future.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the chain keeps its old range and old ways of selling while needs move on. Mechanism: because customers buy from whoever currently meets their needs best, they drift toward sellers with cordless tools and online ordering, so each satisfied customer elsewhere is a sale the chain no longer receives. Consequence: sliding sales and shelves of dated stock - the business that argues with the change is left selling to a shrinking group. Where the chain instead notices early, it gains time to plan: a website, a cordless range, staff trained to advise, each introduced calmly rather than in a rush, which can leave it first with an offering rivals have not matched and its survival secured.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must start from the given position - the range unchanged while needs move. Mechanism: award for the why - customers drift to whichever seller meets the changed need, because the chain no longer matches demand. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - sliding sales - and for its future under an early response: planned action protecting survival.

context.situation: customers shifting to online ordering and cordless tools
facts: customers buying cordless models and ordering online

items.prompt: Explain the elements that make changing customer needs important to a business.
items.canonical_answer: Three elements carry the importance. Sales are at stake: a business that ignores the change risks losing them to rivals that adapted, because customers buy from whoever meets their needs best. Innovation is driven by it: changing needs push businesses to develop new products, and the first to respond owns the new demand. And timing matters: a change recognised early gives the business time to plan, which lowers the risk of a rushed, wrong response. What the parts include is a single pressure - the customer has moved, and the business's sales follow whoever catches up.
marking_guidance: Elements: award one mark for each part - the risk of lost sales, the push toward new products, the value of early recognition - and one mark for what the parts add up to: pressure to adapt or lose customers.

items.prompt: Define a competitive market.
items.canonical_answer: A competitive market is one where many businesses offer similar products to the same customers, so each must work to attract and keep them.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include many sellers of similar products to the same customers, each needing to compete for them. One large business serving a town alone is not a competitive market.

items.prompt: Online sellers have entered Namibia's book market, and a long-established Windhoek bookshop watches its sales slip. Explain how the growth of online selling could lead to tougher competition for the bookshop, and what the outcome could be for the bookshop and its customers.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: online sellers can reach the bookshop's customers from anywhere. Mechanism: because an online business needs relatively little capital - no shopfront on the main road - new entrants appear easily, and because customers can compare prices across sellers in seconds, the bookshop can no longer rely on being the convenient place to browse. Consequence: competition squeezes the shop's sales and margins, while its customers tend to gain lower prices and more choice. The outcome for the business depends on its response - service, author events, same-day delivery of local stock - which decides whether the pressure ends in adaptation or closure; the customers, either way, tend to end up better served.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must start from the given fact of online entry into the market. Mechanism: award for the why - low capital needs bring entrants, and instant price comparison removes the protection of convenience. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - squeezed sales and margins - and for the stakeholder effect on its customers: lower prices and more choice.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main reasons some markets have become more competitive.
items.canonical_answer: Online selling lets a business reach customers anywhere, so distance protects a local seller less than it once did. Starting an online business needs relatively little capital - no prime shopfront, no branch network - so new entrants appear whenever an opportunity shows. Customers can compare prices across many sellers in seconds, which makes it harder for any one business to charge noticeably more for the same thing. And imports widen the choice further, as foreign producers reach customers they once could not. What the reasons include is a common thread: each lowers the barrier between a customer and an alternative seller.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - online reach, low start-up capital, instant price comparison, imports - and one mark for what the reasons include in common: each makes switching to a rival easier.

items.prompt: Define what is meant by a business responding to market change.

items.prompt: Explain how a business could benefit from responding to increased competition by improving the quality of its product.
items.canonical_answer: Improving quality makes the product stand out against the similar offerings rivals sell, so customers are given a reason to choose it beyond price. The benefit develops further: because an improved product is harder to copy than a discount, the business keeps that distinction longer, which leads to steadier sales and customers who return for the quality rather than for a low price. The improvement also supports a firmer price, so the business stays clear of a price war it cannot win.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for quality distinguishing the product from rivals, developed because customers get a reason to choose beyond price, and developed to the consequence - steadier sales and a price the business can defend.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of cutting prices as a response to increased competition.
items.canonical_answer: A price cut reduces the margin on every sale, so the business needs far more customers just to earn what it earned before. Because rivals can match a price within a week, the cut buys little lasting advantage and may start a price war that leaves every business in the market poorer. And customers won on price leave on price: the cut attracts trial, but it does not build the loyalty that protects sales later. The limitation, developed, is that a price cut competes on the one thing rivals copy most easily, so it leads at best to a temporary gain bought with permanent margin.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the reduced margin on every sale, developed because more sales are needed to earn the same total, which leads to the consequence - rivals match the cut and a price war erodes everyone's margins.

items.prompt: Define mass marketing.

items.prompt: Explain the benefits a business gains from mass marketing one product to the whole market.
items.canonical_answer: One product made in huge quantities is cheap to produce and simple to stock, so the business can price within most customers' reach. One promotion campaign covers everyone, so the cost of reaching each customer is small next to a niche's. And a large total market means large total sales from a single design, which spreads the design and promotion costs across many customers. The benefit develops to strategy: a business offering what most customers want at a low price can hold the middle of the market, where the volume sits.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for low cost per item and one wide campaign, developed because production and promotion are shared across all sales, which leads to the consequence - a price most customers accept and large total sales.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of mass marketing for a business whose customers' tastes differ widely.
items.canonical_answer: Where tastes differ widely, one product for everyone fits nobody exactly: each group compromises, which leaves room for a rival to serve one group properly and take it away. The limitation develops: because the mass product aims at the middle, a business that niches any single group better pulls that group out of the mass, and the mass seller cannot answer without giving up the single-product simplicity it was built on. A cheaper copy can also undercut the whole approach, since a product with nothing distinctive about it ends up competing on price alone.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the message fitting no group exactly where tastes differ, developed because each group compromises and a rival can serve one group properly, which leads to the consequence - groups peeled away one at a time.

items.prompt: Gobabis Gem Works makes beaded watchstraps sold to safari guides through three lodges, and posts its new designs to guide forums online. Explain whether this business's approach fits its situation, and what the approach implies for its sales.
items.canonical_answer: The facts here show a niche: a small, clearly defined group - safari guides - reached with a product and promotion designed around their particular tastes, through the lodges and forums where exactly those customers look. The reasoning is that the approach fits, because the group is reachable through those two channels at very low cost and the straps meet the group's wants closely. The implication for sales is the niche's trade: total sales stay modest because the group is small, and the business depends heavily on it - if lodge bookings fall, so does everything else. Conclusion: the approach fits for now, and the owner should watch that dependence rather than assume the niche is safe.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the business's facts - three lodges, guide forums, one product line. Reasoning: award for the link between the narrow group and the low-cost, close-fit approach. Conclusion: award for a judgement on fit that names the dependence risk.

items.prompt: A Keetmanshoop bakery sells one standard loaf to every household in town. A new rival opens selling seeded craft loaves aimed at young professionals, and the bakery's loaf sales begin to slide. Explain how staying with one uniform product could lead to lost sales for the bakery, and how its response could affect its survival.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the bakery keeps one uniform product while a rival niches the young professionals. Mechanism: because the mass loaf fits no group exactly, the group most willing to pay for something better - young professionals - is the easiest to peel away, and the rival's seeded craft loaf answers a want the standard loaf ignores. Consequence: the bakery loses that group's sales first, and they are among its most valuable, so sliding volumes raise the cost of each loaf left. Its survival depends on the response: a craft line of its own protects the volume, and keeping the standard loaf alongside it means the business answers the niche without losing the mass revenue it was built on.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must start from the given position - one uniform product against a niched rival. Mechanism: award for the why - the mass product fits no group exactly, so the group with the strongest want for better bread is lost first. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - the loss of its most valuable sales - and for the survival stakes of the response chosen.

items.prompt: Explain the features that tell niche marketing apart from mass marketing.
items.canonical_answer: The product differs: mass marketing sells one product to the whole market, while niche marketing designs its product around a small, defined group. The promotion differs: one wide campaign against messages placed where the narrow group will see them. The competition faced differs: the mass seller meets rivals head-on across the whole market, while the nicher meets few direct rivals inside its group. And the scale differs: large total sales with a loose fit, against modest total sales with a close one. What the features add up to is a single trade: reach against closeness.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - product, promotion, rivals faced, sales scale - and one mark for what the contrast includes: reach against closeness of fit.

items.prompt: Define market segmentation.
items.canonical_answer: Market segmentation means dividing the market for a product - its actual and potential customers - into groups of similar customers, so each group can be targeted with a product and promotion that suits it.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include dividing the market's customers into groups and targeting each group. Naming one segment, such as teenagers, alone is not the definition.

items.prompt: Explain how a clothing retailer could benefit from segmenting its market before deciding what new lines to stock.
items.canonical_answer: Segmentation divides the retailer's customers into groups of similar shoppers, and each group tells the retailer what to stock: parents buying school-wear, young fashion buyers and older comfort shoppers want different things. The benefit develops: because the retailer can aim its new lines at the group most likely to buy, less stock is bought for shoppers who were never interested, so shelves carry what sells and the promotion reaches likely customers. The result is a range matched to demand, with fewer marked-down leftovers at season's end.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the groups revealing what to stock, developed because lines aimed at the likeliest group sell and promotion reaches likely buyers, which leads to the consequence - fewer unsold lines and less waste.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation for a small business of dividing its market into many segments.
items.canonical_answer: Each segment expects a product and promotion of its own, so costs multiply with every group: separate designs, separate advertising, separate stock. For a small business the limit bites hard, because its budget supports one or two properly served segments at most - and segments served thinly serve nobody well. There is also a size risk: each extra slice is smaller, and a segment too small to cover its own promotion costs becomes a loss dressed up as reach.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for costs multiplying per segment, developed because each group needs its own product and promotion, which leads to the consequence - thinly served segments and slices too small to cover their own costs.

items.prompt: Explain why segmenting the market for a product can lead to more effective promotion.
items.canonical_answer: Because segmentation identifies the group most likely to buy, promotion can be placed where that group looks and worded in the terms it uses, so a bigger share of the budget reaches likely customers and less is spent on people who would not buy. The reason it works is fit: a message written for one defined group says what that group needs to hear, which a message written for everyone cannot. And within each segment the needs are met closely, so the promotion's promise is kept by the product, which supports repeat buying rather than a single trial.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for promotion placed and worded for the likeliest group, because fit raises the share of the budget that reaches likely buyers. Second reason: award for the promise being kept inside the segment, because closely met needs turn advertising into repeat buying.

items.prompt: Define what makes a method of market segmentation appropriate in given circumstances.
items.canonical_answer: A method of segmentation is appropriate in given circumstances when the groups it produces are genuinely different in what they want, large enough to be worth serving, and reachable with the promotion the business can use.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name the three tests - real differences in wants, groups large enough to serve, and groups the business can reach. Naming a method, such as age, without the tests is not the definition.

items.prompt: Windhoek Fit Club plans a fitness app for the whole country and must choose one segmentation method for its launch: by age, by location, or by lifestyle. Its research shows retirees ask for gentle guided routines, students ask for social challenges, and commuters in the capital ask for ten-minute sessions usable between taxis. Consider which method Windhoek Fit Club should use to launch the app.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: launch on lifestyle segmentation. Context: the evidence here is not ages or addresses but wants - gentle routines for retirees, social challenges for students, ten-minute sessions for commuters - and those are lifestyle differences; two commuters of different ages want the same app, so age would group them wrongly. Criterion: the decisive test is which method produces groups genuinely different in what they want from the app, and on this evidence lifestyle separates the recorded wants cleanly, while age would group a retired hiker with a retired non-walker who want opposite things. Counterargument: the case against is cost and reach - lifestyle groups can be harder to identify and target than a simple age filter or a location list, and location at least tells the club which towns to launch in first. Condition: the recommendation depends on the club's tailoring budget; if it can afford one version only, a location-based launch in the capital, where commuters asked most specifically, is the safer first step, with lifestyle as the second release.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation of one method. Context: award for using the case facts - retirees, students, commuters and the wants recorded. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - which method's groups differ in wants. Counterargument: award for the case against the recommendation, such as lifestyle being costlier to target. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated circumstances, such as budget or a location-first launch.

items.prompt: A cereal maker segments by age and serves families with a children's range. Health-conscious older customers start buying a rival's muesli aimed at them, and the maker's family sales flatten. Explain how age-based segmentation failing this group could lead to lost sales, and how re-segmenting by lifestyle could affect the maker's recovery.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the maker's chosen method is age, and the group whose wants changed - health-conscious older customers - does not fit its family range. Mechanism: because the method separates groups by age rather than by what they want from cereal, a group defined by its lifestyle is invisible to it, so the rival that segmented by lifestyle meets a want the maker cannot even name. Consequence: the maker loses those customers, and since its method taught it to watch ages, its own data does not show why the sales left. Recovery: grouping by lifestyle puts health-conscious eaters of all ages into one segment the maker can serve - a muesli line, promotion in the places that group reads - and if that segment is genuinely different in wants, large enough and reachable, the maker regains the lost sales and finishes with a sturdier method than age alone.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must start from the given position - age as the method, a lifestyle group unserved. Mechanism: award for the why - the method is blind to wants that cross age bands, so the lifestyle rival meets a need the maker cannot see. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - lost sales and data that hides the cause - and for the recovery if the lifestyle segment passes the tests of difference, size and reachability.

items.prompt: Explain the features a business looks for when judging whether a method of segmentation is appropriate.
items.canonical_answer: Difference: the groups the method produces must want genuinely different things, or serving them separately adds nothing. Size: each group must be large enough to be worth a product of its own. Reachability: the business must be able to get its promotion to the group through channels it can use. Evidence: the method should be recommended from the business's own sales and research, because it must separate groups the business can actually identify. And revisability: the judgement is not permanent - if the evidence changes, the method should be revisited. What the features include is a decision procedure: test the groups, check the evidence, and stay ready to change.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - difference in wants, size, reachability, evidence, revisability - and one mark for what the set includes: a method judged by whether the business can identify and serve the groups it makes.

items.prompt: The manager of Etosha Outdoor Supplies asks you for advice: cheaper imported brands have entered its market and its regular customers are buying less often. Write several linked points for the manager: state two ways the business could respond to the new competition, each with a reason, and note how each response would affect the business's regular customers.
items.canonical_answer: One response is to improve service - gear fitted properly, advice from staff who know the terrain. Reason: imports can match a price but not knowledge, so service gives regulars a reason to stay beyond price, and it deepens the relationships the newcomers cannot copy. A second response is to adjust the product range toward what the imports do not offer - repairs, locally suitable kit, bundled expeditions. Reason: competing head-on with similar goods invites a price war that cuts the margin on every sale, while a differentiated range moves the contest onto ground the imports have not prepared. For the business's regular customers, better service rewards their loyalty directly and a changed range gives them new reasons to visit - though the manager should check that chasing new lines does not drop the staples the regulars came for. The choice between responses should rest on what the sales records say customers actually value.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each response stated, up to two. Reason: award for the because behind each - service is hard to copy, a differentiated range avoids a price war. Context: award for applying each point to this business and its regular customers rather than in the abstract.

items.prompt: Omaruru Olive Press bottles handmade infused oils and sells 8 000 bottles a year to tourists through guesthouses at N$95 a bottle, at a cost of N$31 a bottle to make. A supermarket chain offers to take 30 000 bottles a year at N$42 each, provided the press blends one standard recipe and labels it for the mass shelf, at an estimated N$26 a bottle to make. Using the figures, consider whether the press should accept the offer.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: each handmade bottle gives a margin of N$64 - N$95 less the N$31 of costs - and on 8 000 bottles that is N$512 000 a year. The standard range would give N$16 a bottle - N$42 less the N$26 - and on 30 000 bottles, N$480 000 a year, so the totals sit close together with the supermarket contract slightly behind. Judgement: decline the offer as it stands. Context: the press is a niche business - a defined group, guesthouse tourists, who pay for handmade character - and the mass deal would trade a N$512 000 niche margin for about N$480 000 of mass margin. Criterion: what decides it is total margin set against what the change would do to the niche, because a standard recipe would blur the very difference guests pay for, so guesthouse sales of the handmade line would likely fall once the same brand sits on a mass shelf. Counterargument: the case for accepting is real - a guaranteed 30 000-bottle order nearly quadruples the press's volume, and the chain opens retail outlets the press cannot reach alone. Condition: the recommendation depends on two checks - whether the press could supply 30 000 bottles without new costs, and whether the chain would accept the standard range under a separate brand; if guesthouse sales are protected by a separate label and capacity is genuinely spare, the balance tips toward accepting.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the offer. Context: award for using the figures - the N$64 and N$16 margins and the yearly totals. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - total margin against the risk to the niche's character and guesthouse sales. Counterargument: award for the case for accepting - guaranteed volume and new outlets. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated checks - capacity costs and brand separation.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "A business should target a niche market rather than the whole market." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the choice: niche marketing targets a small, clearly defined group with a close-fitting product; mass marketing sells one product to the whole market, with reach but a loose fit. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: a niche faces fewer direct rivals and meets its group's wants closely, so loyalty and margins tend to be stronger, and the promotion budget is not spread across people who will never buy. Paragraph 3, the case against: a niche group may be small, so total sales stay modest and the business depends heavily on that one group; the mass market offers large total sales from a single simple product. Paragraph 4, judgement and criterion: the view holds where groups' needs differ sharply and the business's budget is small - the criterion is whether the chosen ground matches the spread of needs the market shows and whether the group is large enough to sustain the business. Recommendation conditional on: the size and reachability of the niche, and on whether the business could later widen from the niche to neighbouring segments without losing the character it built its name on.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach. Context: the plan must use the facts of both approaches - reach against closeness, rival density, dependence. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - the spread of needs in the market against the group's size. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view - small totals and heavy dependence. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated circumstances - size, reachability, room to widen.

items.prompt: Dolomite Cycling, a small Austrian firm, makes one city e-bike sold across Europe. Total sales have been flat for two years, but its service records show two very different groups of repeat buyers: retired customers who ride for leisure and value comfort and step-through frames, and delivery riders who value range, toughness and quick repairs. Analyse the situation and recommend how the firm should segment its market.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the evidence says the one-model approach is holding the firm still - one product for the whole market fits the two recorded groups loosely, because comfort-leisure riders and working delivery riders want opposite things from the same frame. Segmentation benefits the firm directly: dividing its customers into groups of similar riders lets it aim a design and a promotion at each, meeting each group's needs closely, which supports repeat buying in a way one compromise model cannot; the records may also reveal groups no rival serves well. Recommendation: segment by lifestyle - leisure riders against working riders - reached through the channels each group already reads, cycling-club media against courier-firm partnerships. Criterion: the decisive test is difference in wants, and the service records show wants, not ages: a retired courier and a young leisure rider both fit their group by how they use the bike, which age segmentation would blur. Counterargument: two models cost more than one - separate design, stock and promotion - and the firm is small; the case for staying unsegmented is simplicity and a single production line. Condition: the recommendation depends on each segment proving large enough and reachable at a cost the firm can carry, and it should be revisited if the rider mix shifts; launching the working-rider model first in one city, where delivery demand is concentrated, tests the segmentation at the least risk.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation of a segmentation method. Context: award for using the case facts - flat sales, the two groups of repeat buyers and what each values. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - differences in wants shown by use, not age. Counterargument: award for the case against - two products cost a small firm more than one. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated checks - segment size, reachability, a one-city test.
